cells.tense: You're tending what's yours to tend right now, and your hands know it.
cells.ask: Offer up one piece of what you've grown, and let being seen finish it
cells.core:
You're looking after the things that depend on you — the ones you planted, the ones you keep alive — and you're doing it without gripping. Two things need you at once and you're holding both without dropping either. The garden isn't a metaphor to you; it's Tuesday, it's the watering, it's the person who calls and gets answered.

The quiet part is that none of it is a performance. When you let what you've tended be seen, you're not showing off — you're just letting something already finished arrive where it belongs. That letting-be-seen is the next thing this steadiness is free to grow into.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's yours and you let it be seen.
cells.verb: tending what's growing in your care so it comes through whole
cells.place: the place where who you already are becomes visible

lint.detail: the ask carries no word of the place — the same ask would serve any seat

cells.tense: You're already living in how it's all going to look, and the future's the only room you're standing in.
cells.ask: Let one thing you've imagined be enjoyed right now, exactly as it is
cells.core:
You can see where this is all headed, and you're managing the picture in your head harder than the thing in front of you. Every plant gets checked against the harvest, every plan against the version where it worked — and the tending has turned into steering.

The real work looks like care that doesn't exhaust you, holding what you love without clutching at it. Let one thing that's already good stop being a project and just be enjoyed. When you do, you'll find that imagining from a place of having already digested what happened is a different activity than bracing.
cells.sheetLine: You're managing the harvest instead of tending the field.
cells.verb: tending what's growing in your care so it comes through whole
cells.place: the place where who you already are becomes visible

cells.tense: You set something down a while back, and you're still standing at the place you left it.
cells.ask: Let yourself hope out loud about one small thing you're still growing, even if nobody answers
cells.core:
There's a kind of looking-after that stopped happening, and the stopping was quiet enough that you may not have marked it. What's left is a holding pattern — the care isn't gone, it's just not moving toward anything anymore.

When this is working, it doesn't take much. You water one thing because you want it to grow, you wait, you keep wanting it. What brings that back isn't effort pushed at the hollow place — it's hope that's kept going on its own fuel, a small aspiration that outlasts how long it's been. That's what shines: not force, but what kept growing because you kept hoping.
cells.sheetLine: Something small still wants to grow.
cells.verb: tending what's growing in your care so it comes through whole
cells.place: the place where who you already are becomes visible

cells.tense: You're already doing the looking-after — you just haven't put your name on it.
cells.ask: Say out loud that one thing you keep alive is yours to keep alive
cells.core:
You're keeping something alive right now — showing up, tending, holding the thing that needs holding — and you talk about it like it just happens to be that way. You credit the circumstance, the need, the timing. Not yourself.

The care is already real, already doing its work. What's missing is just the acknowledgment — the plain fact that someone is doing this, and that someone is you. When you let the tending be witnessed, release comes more easily: you can finish something and let it go, because the sacrifice was seen. Start by saying the smallest true thing about what you keep alive.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it alive. Say so.
